title: Dynamical Consequences of Nontrivial Topology of Molecular Conical Intersections
authors: Indranil Ghosh, Kush Banker, Gregory S. Engel
abstract: The topology of the electronic structure for an avoided crossing and a conical intersection (CI) is different and is characterized by the presence of the geometric phase in the electronic wavefunction in the latter. Using the linear Jahn-Teller model, we show that an avoided crossing can be created from the conical intersection while preserving the nontrivial topology of the latter by adding a Pauli $σ_y$ term to the Hamiltonian. Analogously to solid state systems, we derive a half-integer topological invariant as the integral of the Berry curvature over the CI nuclear branching space. We investigate the influence of electronic topology on chemical dynamics by conducting fewest-switches surface hopping simulations and find distinct hopping rates on identical eigensurfaces but with different topologies. Our work extends the influence of topology on molecular excited state dynamics beyond the Berry phase that can be practically realized through electron-nuclear and spin-orbit coupling.
summary: This paper explores how the underlying topology of molecular electronic structure, particularly at conical intersections, dictates chemical dynamics. By constructing two Hamiltonians with the same potential energy surfaces but different topological invariants, the authors demonstrate that the topology influences observable nonadiabatic hopping rates via surface hopping simulations. This work establishes topology as a fundamental determinant of molecular excited state relaxation.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the nontrivial topology of molecular conical intersections (CIs) influences nonadiabatic chemical dynamics, extending beyond the standard Berry phase description.
main_result: The authors show that a topological invariant, derived from the Berry curvature, can distinguish between two Hamiltonians ($H_{top}$ and $H_{triv}$) that share identical adiabatic potential energy surfaces, and this difference manifests in measurable, direction-dependent surface hopping rates.
method: The study employs theoretical derivations using the Jahn-Teller model to calculate topological invariants and utilizes Fewest-Switches Surface Hopping (FSSH) simulations to compute nonadiabatic relaxation rates.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using a two-level Jahn-Teller Hamiltonian, comparing a topologically non-trivial version ($H_{top}$) against a trivially gapped counterpart ($H_{triv}$), both exhibiting a CI.
key_observables: Relaxation rates ($R$) of population decay on the upper eigensurface, the topological invariant ($C$), and the Non-Adiabatic Coupling (NAC) vector components.
important_parameters: The coupling strength parameters ($F, \lambda$) and the approach direction ($\hat{Q}_x, \hat{Q}_y$) are crucial for observing the rate differences.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the adiabatic approximation for the FSSH simulation, and the topological invariant is derived from the Berry curvature integral.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the three Hamiltonians (topological, CI, trivial) and their associated geometric structures. Figure 2 shows the surface hopping kinetics (population decay) for different approach directions and Hamiltonians.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by defining the topological invariant using the Berry curvature in the Jahn-Teller model. It then compares the resulting Hamiltonians ($H_{top}$ vs $H_{triv}$) and uses FSSH simulations to demonstrate that the topological difference leads to distinct, measurable nonadiabatic relaxation rates, particularly along certain nuclear coordinates.
why_interesting: This work directly connects abstract concepts from topological physics (Berry curvature, topological invariants) to concrete, measurable quantities in molecular dynamics (nonadiabatic coupling, reaction rates), providing a powerful diagnostic tool for understanding excited state dynamics.
